extraction.name: XTREME-S
extraction.description: Cross-lingual Transfer Evaluation of Multilingual Encoders for Speech: a benchmark covering 102 languages from more than 10 language families, three speech domains, and seven downstream tasks across speech recognition, speech-to-text translation, speech classification, and speech retrieval. It combines FLEURS, Multilingual LibriSpeech, VoxPopuli, CoVoST-2, and MINDS-14.
extraction.license: Tasks are selected to be available under permissive licenses allowing use and redistribution for research purposes; specific licenses are not identified in the paper.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Ankur Bapna, Yu Zhang, Min Ma, Patrick von Platen, Anton Lozhkov, Colin Cherry, Ye Jia, Clara Rivera, Mihir Kale, Daan Van Esch, Vera Axelrod, Simran Khanuja, Jonathan H. Clark, Orhan Firat, Michael Auli, Sebastian Ruder, Jason Riesa, Melvin Johnson
extraction.inLanguage: 102 languages spanning more than 10 language families; language names and ISO codes are listed in Table 8.
extraction.citeAs: Alexis Conneau et al. XTREME-S: Evaluating Cross-lingual Speech Representations. arXiv:2203.10752v3 [cs.CL], 13 April 2022.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: XTREME-S groups existing multilingual datasets—MLS, VoxPopuli, CoVoST-2, and MINDS-14—and introduces FLEURS. For FLEURS, the authors use 2,009 n-way parallel sentences from the publicly available FLoRes development and development-test sets in 102 languages and collect between one and three speech recordings per sentence, averaging 2.3 recordings. MLS uses official 10-hour training splits; VoxPopuli uses the 14 ASR languages with more than 10 hours of labeled data; CoVoST-2 includes all 21 translation directions into English.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Physical data collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: FLEURS is described as more than 97% complete. Table 12 explicitly mentions missing recordings that may be addressed in a second dataset version.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: FLEURS recordings are based on 2,009 parallel sentences from the FLoRes development and development-test sets. MLS is derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox. VoxPopuli contains European Parliament speech, transcriptions, and translations. CoVoST-2 supplies multilingual speech-to-English translation data. MINDS-14 supplies spoken examples of 14 intents from the e-banking domain in 14 language varieties. FLEURS retrieval additionally uses 100,000 in-language sentences from Wikipedia or CommonCrawl as transcription candidates.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: FLEURS is divided into new train, development, and test splits containing 1,509, 150, and 350 source sentences, respectively, with training speakers distinct from development/test speakers. MINDS-14 monolingual datasets are merged into one multilingual dataset and divided into 30% training, 20% development, and 50% test sets. FLEURS language identification uses the same splits as ASR. Optional retrieval uses FLEURS in five languages and augments each language's candidate pool with 100,000 sentences from Wikipedia or CommonCrawl.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The benchmark selects the official MLS 10-hour splits, the 14 VoxPopuli ASR languages with more than 10 hours of data, and all 21 CoVoST-2 translation directions into English. Download and preprocessing-reproduction scripts are provided when needed, but specific audio-cleaning or normalization procedures are not described.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: FLEURS associates collected speech recordings with the corresponding FLoRes sentences for speech recognition and speech-text retrieval; its language-identification task uses the 102 language classes. VoxPopuli provides existing speech transcriptions and translations, CoVoST-2 provides translations into English, and MINDS-14 provides 14 e-banking intent categories. The paper does not describe human annotation or verification procedures.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: FLEURS may receive a second version with missing recordings added and low-quality recordings replaced; updates will be made on the authors' platform. Average results are not expected to change significantly. Additional test sets may be added to confirm submission generalization. More submission details will be added to the XTREME-S dataset card, and retrieval results will be updated in a subsequent paper version. No fixed update schedule or deprecation policy is stated.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speech language is represented across 102 languages. Languages and results are grouped into seven geographical areas: Western Europe, Eastern Europe, Central Asia/Middle East/North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and CJK. FLEURS distinguishes training speakers from development/test speakers.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark aims to accelerate data-efficient multilingual speech technology, particularly for under-represented and low-resource languages. The paper motivates this work as giving speakers of under-represented languages an equal voice on the Internet and helping make their content and culture accessible outside their language communities. Compute-efficient evaluation is intended to make the benchmark accessible to practitioners with limited resources.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper reports stronger baseline performance for Western European languages than for some other geographical groups and attributes this in part to larger amounts of unlabeled Western European speech in MLS and VoxPopuli. Speech translation baselines also perform substantially better on high-resource languages than on low-resource languages. Reducing these geographical and resource-related performance gaps is identified as an important research direction.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The tasks focus on linguistic aspects of speech and do not evaluate nonlinguistic or paralinguistic aspects relevant to speech synthesis or voice conversion. FLEURS is more than 97% complete, with missing and low-quality recordings potentially addressed in a later version. Speech classification is prone to overfitting because inputs contain speaker, domain, and recording-condition information while output label sets are small. Publicly accessible test sets create a risk of inadvertent test-set overfitting. Speech retrieval is a new, optional task, and its baseline results are not yet reported.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, fine-tuning, validation, and testing of multilingual speech representations for ASR, speech-to-English translation, language identification, e-banking intent classification, and optional speech-text retrieval. Multilingual fine-tuning is encouraged to reduce evaluation cost. Hyperparameter search and checkpoint selection should use development sets, with final performance reported on test sets; classification results should preferably be averaged over five random seeds. ASR fine-tuning should use only the benchmark tasks' ASR supervision, although the three ASR datasets may be combined. Additional unlabeled data are allowed. Speech translation may use explicitly documented, publicly accessible text-to-text translation supervision. Classification may use task text during training but not inference, with no other supervision allowed. Language-model decoding is permitted, but results without language-model fusion must also be reported and the model and training data documented. Additional data and methods should be reproducible and accessible, with proprietary large-scale pretraining potentially considered as a separate track.
